headline: Zuckerberg: Closed AI models are a strategic dead end, Meta's future is open
summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared closed AI models a strategic dead end, stating Meta's future is open. This commitment is evident in the Quest platform's open ecosystem, fostering innovation from small studios globally.
details: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently told the Financial Times that closed AI models represent a strategic dead end for the industry. He emphasized that Meta's future strategy is firmly rooted in openness, a stance that quickly garnered significant attention on Hacker News.

This philosophy isn't new for Meta; the company has been cultivating an open platform for years with its Quest VR ecosystem. Features like an open store, OpenXR support, and sideloading options demonstrate a commitment to avoiding gatekeepers.

Such openness directly enabled a two-person studio in India to develop 'AmblyoPunch,' a VR vision-training game for amblyopia. This innovative game was able to launch globally on day one, showcasing the power of an accessible platform.

Amblyopia, commonly known as 'lazy eye,' affects about 3% of the global population. Traditional treatments, often involving patching the stronger eye for hours daily, suffer from low compliance rates among both children and adults.

AmblyoPunch addresses this by using dichoptic rendering, where each eye receives a different contrast Gabor pattern. This forces the brain to fuse both images to play the game, turning therapy into an engaging experience of punching coins and dodging spikes.

headline_marked: [[AI agent Kyboro does real work on your PC]]: 5 critical issues fixed during development
headline: AI agent Kyboro does real work on your PC: 5 critical issues fixed during development
summary: Kyboro is an AI agent that executes tasks directly on your machine, from opening browsers to editing files. Its developer shares the 5 major technical hurdles overcome to make it reliable.
details: Kyboro is an AI agent designed to execute tasks directly on your machine, rather than just suggesting actions. It can open browsers, edit files, and run terminal commands based on plain English descriptions, even with typos.

Early development faced timeout issues where outer layers would give up before inner commands finished, causing tasks to vanish. The fix involved a strict timeout hierarchy: shell < socket < cloud, ensuring inner layers fail first and report errors.

Another challenge was identifying stuck agents that would retry with minor variations, making each attempt seem new. This was resolved by hashing each tool call with all its arguments, allowing for consistent tracking despite small changes.

Sensitive actions like deleting files or making payments require user confirmation, but the cloud-based decision-making and desktop user location created a communication gap. A dedicated 'confirm bridge' was implemented, with a rule that 'no answer equals no action'.

Browser automation proved tricky, as element.click() from injected JavaScript is often ignored, and many buttons reside in inaccessible shadow DOMs. The solution involved using trusted input via the Chrome DevTools Protocol and selectors capable of piercing shadow roots.

Frequent UI fixes typically demand full reinstallations, which can hurt user retention. Kyboro addresses this by updating UI files via content hashes, pulling only changed components on launch. However, elements bundled within Electron still require a full release.
Kyboro is currently available for Windows and Mac, along with a Chrome extension. The developer is actively seeking user feedback on real-world tasks to identify and fix further breaking points.
